summary: Specifies a simple, generic RTP payload format for carrying any non-multiplexed MPEG-4 elementary stream. MPEG-4 compresses audio-visual content into elementary streams, and this format lets them travel over RTP. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3640 gives RTP a way to carry MPEG-4 content of any kind. Each packet says what it holds, how long each piece is and when it should be played, so the receiver can sort the pieces back into order even if the network delivers them out of sequence.

questions: how to stream mpeg-4 elementary streams
what is an access unit in mpeg-4
subtitle: A general way to carry any MPEG-4 audio, video or systems stream over RTP.

tldr.problem: MPEG-4 produces elementary streams of audio frames, video pictures and system commands. Carrying them over RTP needs a way to say what is inside each packet, how big it is, when it should play, and where it belongs in the decoding order.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a payload made of three sections: a header section with one small header per access unit, an optional auxiliary section, and a data section holding the access units themselves. The sizes of the header fields are negotiated up front through MIME format parameters.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard from November 2003 and was later updated by RFC 5691. It defines five modes, from a fully generic one to dedicated ones for CELP and AAC audio, so a simple receiver can be built for one kind of stream.

facts.label: Payload sections
facts.value: 3: AU Header, Auxiliary, Access Unit Data

today: RFC 3640 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2003. It was later updated by RFC 5691; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: What MPEG-4 Elementary Streams Are
sections.content:
The MPEG committee is Working Group 11 of ISO/IEC JTC1 SC29, which specified the MPEG-1, MPEG-2 and, more recently, the MPEG-4 standards. MPEG-4 specifies compression of audio-visual data into, for example, an audio or video elementary stream. In the MPEG-4 standard these streams take the form of audio-visual objects that may be arranged into an audio-visual scene by means of a scene description, and each elementary stream consists of a sequence of Access Units, an audio frame or a video picture being the usual examples.

This specification defines a general and configurable payload structure to transport MPEG-4 elementary streams, in particular MPEG-4 audio including speech streams, MPEG-4 video streams and also MPEG-4 systems streams such as BIFS, OCI, OD and IPMP streams. The payload is simple to implement and reasonably efficient, and it allows for optional interleaving of Access Units to increase error resilience in packet loss.

Some types of MPEG-4 elementary stream include crucial information whose loss cannot be tolerated. RTP does not provide reliable transmission, so receipt of that information is not assured, and the payload specifies how stream state is conveyed so that the receiver can detect the loss of crucial information and cease decoding until the next random access point has been received. Applications transmitting streams with crucial information, such as OD commands, BIFS commands or programmatic content such as MPEG-J and ECMAScript, should include random access points at a suitable periodicity, depending on the probability of loss. An example is the carousel mechanism defined in MPEG-4. Such applications may also use additional protocols to reduce the probability of loss, such as payload formats for retransmission or forward error correction, employed with due consideration to congestion control, or carrying RTP over TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: MPEG-4 turns a movie into separate streams of audio frames, video pictures and scene commands. This document says how to put those streams into network packets and back together again.

sections.title: Access Units
sections.content:
For carriage of compressed audio-visual data, MPEG defines Access Units. An MPEG Access Unit is the smallest data entity to which timing information is attributed. In the case of audio an Access Unit may represent an audio frame, and in the case of video a picture. Access Units are octet-aligned by definition: if an audio frame is not octet-aligned, up to 7 zero-padding bits MUST be inserted at the end of the frame to achieve octet-aligned Access Units, and MPEG-4 decoders MUST be able to decode AUs in which such padding is applied.

Consistent with the MPEG-4 specification, each MPEG-4 part 2 video Access Unit must include all the coded data of a picture, any video stream headers that may precede the coded picture data, and any video stream stuffing that may follow it, up to but not including the start code indicating the start of a new video stream or the next Access Unit.

It is frequently possible to carry multiple Access Units in one RTP packet. This is particularly useful for audio: when AAC is used for encoding a stereo signal at 64 kbits per second, AAC frames contain on average approximately 200 octets, so on a LAN with a 1500 octet MTU an average of 7 complete AAC frames can be carried per RTP packet. Access Units may have a fixed size in octets, but a variable size is also possible. To facilitate parsing when multiple Access Units are concatenated in one RTP packet, the size of each AU is made known to the receiver. With a constant AU size the size is communicated out of band through a MIME format parameter; with variable size AUs the RTP payload carries an in-band AU size field for each contained AU. In combination with the RTP payload length, the size information lets the receiver split the payload back into the individual AUs. To simplify receiver implementations, when multiple AUs are carried in an RTP packet each AU MUST be complete, and an AU MUST NOT be repeated in other RTP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: An Access Unit is the smallest piece of the stream that gets a timestamp, such as one audio frame. Several of them can travel in one packet, and the packet says how big each one is so the receiver can split them apart.

sections.title: The Three Sections of the Payload
sections.content:
The RTP payload following the RTP header contains three octet-aligned data sections, of which the first two MAY be empty. The first is the AU Header Section, which contains one or more AU-headers, each of which MAY be empty, in which case the entire AU Header Section is empty. The second is the Auxiliary Section, containing auxiliary data, which may also be configured empty. The third is the Access Unit Data Section, containing either a single fragment of one Access Unit or one or more complete Access Units, and it MUST NOT be empty.

The AU Header Section consists of the AU-headers-length field followed by a number of AU-headers. The AU-headers are configured using MIME format parameters and MAY be empty; if the AU-header is configured empty the AU-headers-length field SHALL NOT be present and the whole section is empty. If it is not empty, the AU-headers-length is a two octet field giving the length in bits of the following AU-headers, excluding the padding bits. Each AU-header is associated with a single Access Unit or fragment contained in the Access Unit Data Section of the same RTP packet, and the AU-headers are bit-wise concatenated in the order in which the Access Units appear in the data section, so the n-th AU-header refers to the n-th AU or fragment. If the concatenated AU-headers consume a non-integer number of octets, up to 7 zero-padding bits MUST be inserted at the end to achieve octet alignment.

The Auxiliary Section consists of the auxiliary-data-size field followed by the auxiliary-data field. Receivers MAY parse the auxiliary-data field, and the auxiliary-data-size field indicates its length in bits so that receivers can skip it without parsing. The coding of the auxiliary data is not defined by the document, and auxiliary information MUST NOT be transmitted until its format, meaning and signalling have been specified. Receivers without knowledge of such data MUST skip the auxiliary data field.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has up to three parts: a list of small headers, an optional block for data this document does not define, and the media itself. The headers are optional too, so a simple stream can use almost the whole packet for data.

sections.title: What Each AU-header Can Say
sections.content:
Each AU-header may contain the fields AU-size, AU-Index or AU-Index-delta, CTS-flag, CTS-delta, DTS-flag, DTS-delta, RAP-flag and Stream-state, in that mutual order. The length in bits of the fields, except the three flags, is defined by MIME format parameters, and if a parameter has the default value of zero the associated field is not present. The number of bits used for a present field MUST be chosen large enough to correctly encode the largest value of that parameter during the session. In the general case a receiver can only discover the size of an AU-header by parsing it, since the presence of the CTS-delta and DTS-delta fields is signalled by the value of the flags.

AU-size indicates the size in octets of the associated Access Unit in the same packet. When the AU-size is associated with a fragment, it indicates the size of the entire AU and not of the fragment, and the size of the fragment is known from the size of the data section. AU-Index indicates the serial number of the associated Access Unit or fragment, incremented by 1 for each consecutive AU in decoding order; it occurs only in the first AU-header of the section, and later headers use AU-Index-delta, which gives the difference from the previous AU so that the serial number of the n-th AU is the serial number of the n-1st plus the delta plus 1. A delta of 0 means the Access Units are consecutive in decoding order, while a larger value signals that interleaving is applied.

CTS-flag says whether the CTS-delta field is present, and CTS-delta encodes the composition time stamp as a two's complement offset from the RTP header timestamp. DTS-flag and DTS-delta do the same for the decoding time stamp, as an offset from the CTS. MPEG-4 defines two kinds of timestamp: the composition time stamp represents the sampling instant of an AU and is equivalent to the RTP timestamp, while the decoding time stamp may be used in video streams that use bi-directional coding, and cannot be carried in the RTP header. RAP-flag, when set to 1, indicates that the Access Unit provides a random access point to the content of the stream, and if an Access Unit is fragmented the flag MUST be 0 for each non-first fragment. Stream-state specifies the state of the stream for an AU of an MPEG-4 system stream, and when the stream state changes the value MUST be incremented by one.
sections.plainLanguage: Each small header can say how big the piece is, which piece it is in the decoding order, when it should be shown, and whether the decoder can start from it. Which of these are present, and how many bits each takes, is agreed up front.

sections.title: Interleaving to Survive Packet Loss
sections.content:
When an RTP packet carries a contiguous sequence of Access Units, the loss of such a packet can result in a decoding gap for the user. One method of alleviating this problem is to allow the Access Units to be interleaved in the RTP packets, which for a modest cost in latency and implementation complexity achieves significant error resilience to packet loss. To support optional interleaving, the payload allows index information to be sent for each Access Unit. After informing receivers about the buffer resources to allocate for de-interleaving, the sender is free to choose the interleaving pattern without propagating it in advance, and could adjust it dynamically based on Access Unit size or error rate. The receiver does not need to know the pattern used; it only needs to extract the index information and insert the Access Unit into the appropriate place in the decoding or rendering queue.

For example, if an RTP packet contains 3 Access Units numbered 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on, and an interleaving group length of 9 is chosen, then RTP packet 0 contains AUs 0, 3 and 6, packet 1 contains 1, 4 and 7, packet 2 contains 2, 5 and 8, packet 3 contains 9, 12 and 15, and packet 4 contains 10, 13 and 16. A packet SHALL carry either one or more complete Access Units or a single fragment of one Access Unit; fragments of the same Access Unit have the same timestamp but different RTP sequence numbers, and the marker bit is 1 on the last fragment of an Access Unit and 0 on the others.

When interleaving is applied, a de-interleave buffer is needed to put the Access Units back into decoding order, and the decoding of early Access Units has to be postponed until all the Access Units that precede them in decoding order are present. The RFC defines the maximum displacement in time of an Access Unit as the maximum difference between the timestamp of an AU in the pattern and the timestamp of the earliest AU that is not yet present. In the example above the maximum displacement equals 5 AU periods, found for AU(6) and AU(7). Senders MUST signal the maximum displacement via the MIME format parameter maxDisplacement, and an estimate of the buffer size is that displacement multiplied by the maximum bit rate, divided by the RTP clock frequency.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of putting consecutive pieces in consecutive packets, the sender spreads them out, so losing one packet does not wipe out a whole stretch of sound or video. The receiver sorts them back using the index numbers, and needs a buffer to hold the early arrivals until their turn comes.

sections.title: Modes and Their Signalling
sections.content:
While it is possible to build fully configurable receivers capable of receiving any MPEG-4 stream, the specification also allows simplified, dedicated receivers, for example capable of receiving only one type of MPEG-4 stream. This is achieved by requiring that specific modes be defined in order to use the specification, and the applied mode MUST be signalled. Signalling matters particularly for receivers that can only decode one or more specific modes, since they need to know whether the applied mode is supported.

The document defines a generic mode that can be used for any MPEG-4 stream, plus modes for MPEG-4 CELP and AAC streams. The generic mode is the most configurable. CELP-cbr carries one or more complete CELP frames of fixed size, with no interleaving and no fragmentation; both the AU Header Section and the Auxiliary Section MUST be empty, and the constantSize parameter carries the frame length. CELP-vbr carries complete CELP frames of variable size with optional interleaving; because CELP frames are very small there is no support for fragmenting them, and the AU-size field is coded with 6 bits with 2 bits for the index. AAC-lbr carries one or more complete AAC frames of variable size, with interleaving allowed and therefore de-interleaving required; the maximum size of an AAC frame in this mode is 63 octets and frames MUST NOT be fragmented. AAC-hbr carries variable size AAC frames, either one or more complete frames or a single fragment, again with interleaving allowed; the maximum size of an AAC frame is 8191 octets, which requires 13 bits for the size and 3 bits for the index, so each AU-header is 2 octets.

Additional modes are expected to be defined in future RFCs, and each must be in full compliance with the specification. A mode MUST NOT specify new default values for MIME parameters, and the MIME parameters that configure the RTP payload MUST be present unless they have the default value. The signalling itself is carried in MIME format parameters conveyed to the receiver via SDP, or through other means. The MIME subtype name is mpeg4-generic, and the media type is video for MPEG-4 Visual streams, audio for MPEG-4 Audio streams, and application for MPEG-4 Systems streams that serve purposes other than an audio-visual presentation.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is designed so a receiver can be built for just one kind of stream. Five modes are defined, from a general one to ones tuned for constant-rate speech, variable-rate speech, low-bitrate AAC and high-bitrate AAC. The sender says which mode it is using before the stream starts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RTP packets using this payload format are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification, which implies that confidentiality of the media streams is achieved by encryption. Because the data compression used with this payload format is applied end to end, encryption may be performed on the compressed data, so there is no conflict between the two operations. The packet processing complexity of this payload type, excluding media data processing, does not exhibit any significant non-uniformity on the receiver side to cause a denial-of-service threat.

However, it is possible to inject non-compliant MPEG streams, audio, video and systems, so that the receiver or decoder's buffers are overloaded, which might compromise the functionality of the receiver or even crash it. This is especially true for end-to-end systems like MPEG, where the buffer models are precisely defined. MPEG-4 Systems supports stream types including commands that are executed on the terminal, such as OD commands and BIFS commands, and programmatic content like MPEG-J and MPEG-4 scripts, and it is possible to use one or more of these in a non-compliant manner to crash the receiver or make it temporarily unavailable. Senders that transport MPEG-4 content SHOULD ensure that such content is MPEG compliant, and receivers that support MPEG-4 content should prevent malfunctioning of the receiver in case of non-compliant content. Authentication mechanisms can be used to validate the sender and the data to prevent security problems due to non-compliant malignant MPEG-4 streams.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypting the stream is what protects it. The format itself does not make the receiver's work uneven, but a stream that breaks the rules of MPEG-4 can still overload or crash a decoder, so senders and receivers both need to check what they are carrying.

THE FIVE MODES DEFINED BY THIS RFC

items.label: CONSTANT BIT-RATE CELP
items.desc: Complete CELP frames of fixed size. No interleaving, no fragmentation.

items.label: VARIABLE BIT-RATE CELP
items.desc: Complete CELP frames of variable size, with optional interleaving.

items.label: LOW BIT-RATE AAC
items.desc: Complete AAC frames of variable size, at most 63 octets, never fragmented.

items.label: HIGH BIT-RATE AAC
items.desc: Complete or fragmented AAC frames of variable size, at most 8191 octets.
